summary: A satirical, whimsical walk through the public works regulatory process in a local government after September 1, 2023, following a series of fictionalized-sounding characters through approvals, permits, budgeting, contracts, compliance, change orders, paving and final inspection. The piece pokes fun at bureaucratic complexity, centered on a sprawling regulatory document nicknamed 'The Behemoth.' It draws no conclusions beyond noting the uncertainty and absurdity built into the framework.
one_line: A humorous satirical tour of the bureaucratic stages of public works projects under the City Council's 'Behemoth' regulatory almanac, from approval to punch list.
key_facts: On October 15, 2023, the City Council released the Comprehensive Public Works Regulatory Almanac, nicknamed 'The Behemoth' and said to be read by only three people.
The Behemoth was authored by city clerk Bartholomew Bureaucrat III and purports to simplify the approval process.
In December 2023, Emily Engineer submitted a blueprint for a bridge over Troubled Creek and faced review by Environmental, Structural, Aesthetic and Historical Preservation committees.
In January 2024, city planner Paul Paperwork was stuck navigating 'Permit Purgatory,' involving zoning rules and code inspectors to obtain a construction permit.
In March 2024, Councilman Rich PennyPincher suggested making roads narrower to save on asphalt.
On April Fool's 2024, the Department of Public Works accidentally awarded a major city park renovation contract to a company specializing in balloon animal artistry.
The minutes of that contract meeting were reportedly classified out of embarrassment rather than privacy.
In summer 2024, project manager Sarah Supervisor struggled with compliance, and a bookie on Fifth Street was rumored to be taking bets on whether projects would pass inspection.
In September 2024, site foreman Joe Jackhammer received the 23rd change order, a record beating the previous year's 22.
Change orders included rerouting sewer lines for the Society for Subterranean Ecology and building barriers that don't offend local graffiti artists.
Regulation 4.2.3.b renames shovels as 'manually operated subgrade excavation devices.'
In November 2024, painter Pablo Paveway striped the road, with the Color Coordination Committee requiring a specific 'eggshell white.'
Inspector Ira Incisive oversees the final punch list, where any imperfection can send a project back to purgatory.
